title: Ultrasonic Testing for Shipyards | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US shipyards, ports and vessels: hull weld UT, plate checks and thickness readings, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Shipyards, Vessels and Ports in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT provides on-site ultrasonic testing (UT) for shipyards, repair yards, port terminals and vessel owners across the United States: weld examination on hull, deck and tank structure, plate and lamination checks, and thickness readings on steel that has been in salt water for years. Technicians are mobilized to the yard or pier for the agreed scope. To get a quote, request a UT inspection quote with the drawings, weld map and the specification that governs the work.

What ultrasonic testing is used for on ships and marine structures

A ship is a welded steel structure that flexes in a seaway, sits in a corrosive electrolyte and is repaired many times during its life. UT answers two different questions on that structure. The first is whether a weld or a plate contains a planar or volumetric flaw below the surface. The second is how much steel remains, which is a thickness question. Both use the same sound-based physics, but they are different examinations with different procedures, different calibration blocks and different people deciding what the result means.

Weld examination typically concerns shell and deck butt seams, longitudinal and transverse stiffener connections, bulkhead boundaries, tank-top and hopper-knuckle details, crane pedestals, and the thick welded sections of rudder stocks, skegs and stern-frame fabrications. Thickness readings concern wasted plating, tank-boundary corrosion, deck plating under cargo gear and the shell near the waterline. On a newbuild, the examination is part of the builder's quality plan. On a repair, it often sets the scope: the readings and the flaw map tell the owner and the surveyor how much steel to crop and renew.

US rules that drive the examination

For US-flag commercial vessels, the US Coast Guard rules in 46 CFR govern construction, inspection and repair, including the welding and piping requirements in the marine engineering subchapter. Most commercial hulls are also built and maintained to the rules of a classification society, and those rules set the survey intervals and the acceptance of steel renewals. Weld inspection requirements normally come from the contract specification, which may reference the society's rules for materials and welding, AWS D3.5 for hull welding practice, or ASME Section V for the examination method itself. Navy work is governed by NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 as the controlling document for nondestructive testing; Atlantis names it here only as the document that governs that work and does not claim NAVSEA qualification.

Who accepts or rejects an indication matters as much as who finds it. Our technician performs the examination and reports against the criterion in your specification. The owner's representative, the yard's quality department or the class surveyor decides on repair, acceptance or deferral. We do not set acceptance limits of our own.

Weld inspection on hull, deck and tank structure

Shear-wave contact UT is the standard way to look inside a thick butt or tee weld on plate, with angle selection based on the bevel geometry and plate thickness. The technique follows the method requirements in ASME Section V, Article 4, and the acceptance criterion comes from the governing code. Each examination starts with a procedure that fixes the search unit angle, frequency, scan pattern and reference level. Calibration is checked on a block of similar acoustic properties, before the work, at intervals through the shift and at the end.

Several shipyard conditions change how the work is planned. Weld caps are often left unground, so the surface is rough and the probe must be coupled with a viscous couplant. Plate with rolled lamination can mask the weld volume, so a straight-beam scan of the plate beside the weld precedes the angle-beam scan. Tanks and voids need confined-space entry, ventilation, gas testing and a rescue plan owned by the yard or vessel; our technicians work to that permit. For a closer look at the sibling jobs, see our page on ultrasonic weld inspection, which covers the examination in more depth for any industry.

UT cannot reliably find every flaw type. Very small surface-breaking cracks are better located by the surface methods, and some flat, tight lack-of-fusion planes sit at angles that a single beam angle can miss. Where a detail has a history of toe cracking, we recommend pairing UT with magnetic particle inspection, and on non-ferrous or stainless parts with liquid penetrant testing. Radiography is not part of this offer: Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography here is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules.

Thickness gauging on hull plating, tanks and decks

Thickness readings are taken with a digital gauge and a dual-element or single-element probe, depending on the surface. The method is described in ASTM E797 for manual contact measurement, and ASME Section V, Article 5 covers thickness measurement as an examination method. The gauge is calibrated on steel of known thickness and velocity; a velocity check on the actual material avoids the systematic error that comes from assuming a velocity that does not match the plate.

The surface decides the quality of the reading. Pitted plate gives scattered values, because the back wall is irregular and the probe sees the nearest peak. Heavy scale or paint thicker than the gauge can compensate for adds a bias, so the technician either removes the coating at the reading points or uses a gauge mode designed for it, and records which. We take readings on a grid agreed with the owner, with closer spacing where wastage is seen, and sketch the grid and the lowest values on the report. The grid fixes the repeatable points, so a survey two years later can be compared point to point.

A word on class credit. For class-credited ship thickness gauging, Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. Until a certificate is issued, readings we take are for the owner's own decisions, not for credit to a class survey. That covers pre-docking steel estimates, condition assessment for purchase or charter, between-survey checks and repair-scope planning. For the full maritime scope, including ports outside the contiguous United States and Europe, see the maritime inspection section.

Port cranes, pedestals and waterfront structures

Shore-side steel near the water has the same corrosion pressure as the ship. Container and ship-to-shore crane booms, portal and pedestal cranes governed by ASME B30.4, runway beams, bollard foundations and fender systems all carry welded structure that is loaded in fatigue. The owner's inspection program sets what is examined and how often. Our UT work on these structures focuses on the high-stress welds at boom hinges, trolley rails, pedestal-to-deck connections and the base plate welds under the slewing ring.

Port access adds its own demands. Technicians need a TWIC card for unescorted access to secured areas of a regulated facility, and the terminal may require its own safety orientation, fall-protection plan and lock-out of the crane before anyone climbs it. Scaffold or access platforms are normally provided by the facility. Lifting hardware and hooks are better examined with the surface method; see our page on magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment.

Techniques that show up in the details

  • Couplant: a gel or oil that stays put on vertical shell and overhead deck surfaces, with a note of the product used so the report can be repeated.
  • Surface temperature: standard probes and couplants tolerate a limited range, so hot work or sun-heated deck plate is cooled or measured with a high-temperature probe and couplant combination.
  • Reference level and scan gain: set on a calibration block in the same thickness range as the plate, with an agreed scanning gain above reference.
  • Coverage: a weld is scanned from both sides where geometry allows. Where it does not, the report says so and names what was not covered.
  • Replacement plate: new insert plate is scanned for lamination before it is welded in, because a flaw found afterwards means a second cut.

What the report contains

Every examination ends with a written report that someone else can read and repeat. It identifies the vessel or structure, the component and its location by frame number, drawing reference or weld number. It names the procedure and revision, the specification and acceptance criterion, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and the surface condition. It lists the technician and qualification level, with the Level III who reviewed the report. Indications are recorded by location, length and amplitude relative to reference, with an accept or reject entry against the named criterion. Thickness work adds the grid sketch, the lowest reading in each zone and the nominal thickness used for comparison.

What to send for a quote

  • Vessel type and the yard, pier or terminal where the work will take place
  • Drawings, weld maps or the thickness-gauging plan, with quantities and the governing specification or class requirement
  • Plate material and thickness range, and whether coatings are to be removed
  • Access arrangements, confined-space permits, TWIC requirements and any hot-work restrictions
  • The deadline set by the vessel schedule, so we can tell you honestly whether the scope fits it

Where we work in the US marine market

We mobilize to yards and ports on all three coasts. The pages below describe UT in each of these port cities.

  • Norfolk: the largest concentration of ship repair and Navy work on the Atlantic coast.
  • Pascagoula: Gulf Coast shipbuilding with heavy plate fabrication and long weld runs.
  • Mobile: aluminum and steel vessel construction on Mobile Bay.
  • San Diego: Pacific repair and Navy ship maintenance.
  • Seattle: ferries, fishing fleet and Puget Sound repair yards.
  • Tacoma: container terminal cranes and tug and barge repair.
  • New Orleans: river terminals and Mississippi barge fleets.
  • Baltimore: the Chesapeake shipyards and bulk terminals.
  • Jacksonville: ship repair and cargo terminals on the St. Johns River.
  • Charleston: container port cranes and shipyard steel.

Training your own technicians

Many yards qualify their own people under a written practice. Atlantis offers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with the ultrasonic simulator for practice before the hands-on work. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, not the course provider. Our maritime NDT training page describes the programs for marine employers, and the national ultrasonic testing page covers what UT is, and what it is not, for every industry.

What we do not do here

We do not perform radiography in the United States. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not act as class surveyor or issue class certificates. We do not calculate remaining life or approve repairs; the owner's engineer or surveyor does that from our data. Our UT supports the decision with a clear record, and the decision remains yours.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness readings that count for a class survey?
faq.a: Not yet. Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. Until a certificate is issued, our readings are for the owner's own decisions, not for credit to a class survey. They are useful for pre-docking estimates, condition checks and repair planning.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT on a hull weld program?
faq.a: Send the drawings or weld map, the number and length of welds, plate thickness and material, the governing specification, access arrangements, confined-space and TWIC requirements, and the dates set by the vessel schedule. With that we can scope the work and state what is out of scope.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is accepted or rejected?
faq.a: The acceptance criterion comes from your specification, class rules or the NAVSEA document where the contract names it. Our technician records indications against that criterion, and the owner's representative, yard quality department or surveyor decides on repair or acceptance.

faq.q: Can UT inspect aluminum hull and superstructure welds?
faq.a: It can on sufficiently thick sections, but it needs a procedure written for the alloy and the geometry, with calibration blocks of matching material. Thin aluminum plate is often better served by liquid penetrant testing for surface cracks.

faq.q: Do your technicians need a TWIC card?
faq.a: Technicians who need unescorted access to secured areas of a regulated port or facility must hold a TWIC. Tell us at quoting time which gates and areas are involved, and we will plan access with the facility security officer.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing better than magnetic particle inspection on a ship weld?
faq.a: They answer different questions. UT looks inside the weld volume and measures remaining steel; magnetic particle inspection finds surface and near-surface cracks on ferritic steel. Critical details often get both.

faq.q: Do you offer radiography for shipyard welds?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules. UT is the volumetric method we offer, where your code and your owner allow it in place of radiography.

faq.q: Can you gauge tank boundaries while the tank is in service?
faq.a: Readings from outside the tank are possible where the surface is accessible and the plate is not coated beyond what the gauge can handle. Entry into cargo or ballast tanks needs a permit, gas freeing and rescue arrangements that the vessel or yard controls.

faq.q: What is in the thickness report for a hull survey?
faq.a: The report lists the vessel, frame or location references, nominal and measured thickness, the grid sketch, the instrument, probe and calibration block, couplant, surface condition, the technician and level, and the Level III reviewer.
